title: Episode 105: The Wreck of the Royal Tar: The Circus Menagerie Ship Disaster
description:
In October 1836, the steamship Royal Tar caught fire in a howling gale off the coast of Maine while transporting a traveling circus menagerie. Trapped between raging flames and icy seas were ninety-three passengers, an elephant, two camels, royal Bengal tigers, and dancing bears.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we sail into the stormy, fog-choked waters of Penobscot Bay, Maine, on an October afternoon in eighteen thirty-six, to witness one of the most bizarre, terrifying, and surreal maritime catastrophes in American history: the burning of the paddle steamer Royal Tar. Loaded with ninety-three passengers and crew, the ship was also transporting the Burgess Collection of exotic animals: a traveling circus menagerie featuring two royal Bengal tigers, a full-grown circus elephant, two African camels, six dancing bears, and an aviary of tropical birds. When the ship's coal-fired boilers ran dry and ignited the wooden hull in a howling autumn gale, passengers were caught between a roaring wall of fire, man-eating carnivores breaking out of wooden cages, and the freezing Atlantic ocean. Here is George with the full, heart-pounding account.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GOLDEN AGE OF TRAVELING MENAGERIES
In the eighteen thirties, long before television, radio, or widespread zoological gardens, ordinary Americans and Canadians living in small provincial towns had never seen living exotic animals from distant continents. The primary window into the natural wonders of the wider world was the traveling menagerie: roaming exhibitions of wild beasts transported in heavy iron-barred wagons that followed stagecoach turnpikes and coastal shipping routes. In early autumn eighteen thirty-six, the celebrated Burgess and Dexter Menagerie completed a triumphant, lucrative summer tour across the Maritime provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, dazzling thousands of pioneer families.
The travelling show was a magnificent zoological circus. Its prized centerpiece was Mogul, a magnificent four-ton Indian elephant who performed tricks and marched in town parades. Alongside Mogul were two royal Bengal tigers, an African lion, two Arabian camels, a leopard, a hyena, six trained European brown bears, a collection of chattering monkeys, and dozens of colorful caged tropical birds and snakes. Accompanied by twenty wagons, sixteen horses, and circus brass bands, the menagerie was preparing to return to the United States for the winter season.
To transport this colossal, exotic entourage across the Bay of Fundy to Portland, Maine, show proprietor Mr. Dexter chartered the steam packet Royal Tar. Built just four years earlier in New Brunswick, the Royal Tar was a two-masted, wooden-hulled sidewheel paddle steamer measuring one hundred and sixty-four feet in length. Powered by a primitive, single-cylinder low-pressure steam engine fed by coal-fired boilers, the ship was considered one of the finest and most modern steam vessels operating along the northeastern Atlantic seaboard. Provincial newspapers had hailed the arrival of the exotic menagerie with breathless excitement, publishing woodcut illustrations of the wild beasts to entice rural farming families.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: A SHIP PACKED TO THE GUNWALES
When the Royal Tar docked at Saint John, New Brunswick, on October twenty-first, eighteen thirty-six, Captain Thomas Reed and his crew were confronted with an overwhelming logistical nightmare. In addition to seventy-two paying civilian passengers—including wealthy merchants, families, women, and sixteen small children—and a crew of twenty-one sailors, the ship had to accommodate the colossal circus menagerie, dozens of heavy animal wagons, and twenty-one horses.
To fit the menagerie aboard, the main deck was transformed into a chaotic floating zoo. Mogul the elephant was tethered securely on the forward open deck, while heavy wooden and iron cages containing the tigers, lion, bears, and hyena were wedged along the gunwales and lashed tightly to deck stanchions. The heavy animal wagons and baggage were stacked on the hurricane deck, completely obstructing access to the ship's two small wooden lifeboats. Furthermore, dozens of bales of hay and dry straw for animal feed were stacked directly adjacent to the boiler room vents and smokestack.
Experienced harbor pilots warned that the vessel was dangerously overloaded and top-heavy, but Captain Reed, anxious to beat approaching winter gales, ordered lines cast off on October twenty-second. The Royal Tar steamed southward into the Bay of Fundy, but was immediately struck by fierce head gales that forced the ship to seek shelter in Eastport, Maine, for two days while high winds howled outside. Bales of combustible dry hay and bedding straw had been crammed into every open corridor between the animal wagons, creating a continuous tinder trail leading straight toward the engine room.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BOILER RUNS DRY OFF VINALHAVEN
On Tuesday morning, October twenty-fifth, eighteen thirty-six, the wind shifted slightly, and Captain Reed resumed the voyage down the rugged, rocky coast of Maine, heading toward Portland. By early afternoon, the Royal Tar was steaming across western Penobscot Bay, about two miles off the isolated island of Vinalhaven, battling rising seas and heavy gusts.
Deep inside the sweltering engine room, an act of catastrophic negligence was unfolding. Second Engineer Thomas Stoddart, who was on duty supervising the boilers, noticed that the water gauge on the boiler was acting erratically due to the violent rolling of the ship in heavy swells. To keep steam pressure high against the wind, Stoddart ordered coal shoveled relentlessly into the fireboxes. However, the boiler's feedwater pump had failed, and because the water level inside the boiler dropped below the crown sheet, the iron plates became red-hot and dry.
At shortly after one o'clock, the intense, radiant heat from the glowing boiler plates ignited the dry wooden bulkheads and structural timbers surrounding the engine room. Dense, suffocating smoke began pouring up through the engine room hatchway onto the main deck. Moments later, tongue of yellow flame leaped outward, igniting the stacked bales of dry hay and straw stored near the smokestack. In an instant, the center of the wooden steamship became a raging furnace. The intense vibration of the primitive single-cylinder steam engine shook the wooden bulkheads continuously, loosening fuel connections and drying out structural timbers.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: FIRE, BEASTS, AND PANIC ON THE MAIN DECK
The fire spread with terrifying, explosive speed through the dry wooden decks, fanned by the howling thirty-mile-per-hour ocean gale. Within minutes, the blaze severed the ship's steering chains, leaving the rudder locked and the vessel spinning helplessly in the trough of heavy sea waves. Worse still, the flames drove the engineers away from the engine controls before they could shut off the steam, leaving the giant paddle wheels churning wildly at full speed, creating an artificial hurricane that drove the flames directly aft toward the crowded passenger cabins.
On deck, pandemonium erupted into a surreal, apocalyptic nightmare. Terrified by the smoke and roaring flames, the caged animals began shrieking, roaring, and throwing themselves against iron bars. The heat scorched the fur of the caged tigers, whose blood-curdling screams mingled with the shrieks of terrified women and children huddled on the stern. The six dancing bears broke out of their burning wooden cages, roaming the smoke-filled deck in frantic circles before leaping overboard into the freezing ocean.
Mogul the elephant, panicked by flames scorching his leathery hide, trumpeted in agony and strained against his heavy ropes. In a frantic bid for survival, the four-ton giant broke his iron chains and charged across the deck, crushing luggage wagons before throwing his massive body over the side into the icy waters of Penobscot Bay. In the sea below, passengers clinging to wooden wreckage watched in terror as tigers, bears, and an enormous elephant swam desperately amidst the freezing ocean swells. The terrified cries of the exotic beasts reverberated across the misty waters of Penobscot Bay, creating an unforgettable and surreal sonic landscape of frontier tragedy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE COWARDICE AND THE CUTTER
As the midsection of the ship burned down to the water, the human struggle for survival took a shameful and dramatic turn. The ship possessed two wooden lifeboats: a small jolly boat and a larger sixteen-man cutter. Instead of organizing an orderly evacuation of women and children, Captain Thomas Reed and sixteen crewmen and able-bodied male passengers seized the large lifeboat, lowered it into the sea, and pulled away from the burning wreck, claiming later that they intended to tow the ship or seek help from the distant shore.
Abandoned on the blazing stern were over sixty helpless passengers—including all the women and sixteen small children—crowded onto a shrinking, burning deck less than twenty feet wide. Desperate mothers tied their infants to wooden boards and tossed them overboard, hoping they would wash ashore on distant island rocks. Men stripped off heavy wool coats and leaped into the forty-five-degree water, only to succumb to hypothermia and drowning within minutes.
Two miles away, anchored in the lee of Fox Island, was the United States Revenue Cutter Morris, commanded by Captain Richard Sturgis. Spotting the colossal column of black smoke rising on the horizon, Sturgis immediately slipped his anchor, hoisted all sail, and bore down on the burning wreck. Because the wind and tide were unfavorable, the Morris could not reach the scene for over an hour, but Sturgis deployed his ship's launches, pulling dozens of freezing survivors from the water and fishing drowning passengers from floating timber. Captain Sturgis and his young revenue cutter crew demonstrated extraordinary seamanship, maneuvering their wooden sailing vessel against adverse tides to pull shivering souls from the surf.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TOLL OF THE MENAGERIE DISASTER
When the smoking keel of the Royal Tar finally hissed beneath the waves of Penobscot Bay late that afternoon, thirty-two human lives had been lost: twenty-nine passengers, including all sixteen children, and three crew members. Sixty-one survivors were pulled alive from the freezing sea by the Revenue Cutter Morris and local island fishermen who sailed out in small dories to assist in the rescue.
For the traveling menagerie, the disaster was total. Every single exotic bird, monkey, camel, and tiger perished, along with the horses and caged beasts. Remarkably, two of the trained European bears managed to swim the two freezing miles to Vinalhaven Island, where bewildered local sheep farmers discovered them days later wandering through coastal pastures. Mogul the elephant, however, was not so fortunate: after swimming gallantly for several hours in the freezing swells, the magnificent creature drowned, his body washing ashore days later on the rocky beaches of Brimstone Island.
The disaster sent shockwaves through Maine and New England. Maritime courts condemned the practice of storing combustible animal feed adjacent to uninsulated boiler flues, and public outrage burned fiercely against Captain Reed for abandoning his passengers in the primary lifeboat. The tragedy led directly to stricter federal maritime safety regulations governing passenger capacities and lifeboat accessibility on coastal steamships. Brave island fishermen launched their modest hand-rowed wooden dories into the rising gale, risking their own lives to search for crying children amidst the smoke and waves.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGEND OF THE CIRCUS SHIP
The bizarre and tragic story of the Royal Tar passed immediately into maritime folklore, inspiring ballads, folk tales, and regional legends that have survived for nearly two centuries along the coast of Maine. For generations, fishermen on Penobscot Bay shared fireside ghost tales of seeing the spectral silhouette of an elephant swimming through the coastal fog off Fox Islands on stormy autumn nights.
In nineteen seventy-five, marine archaeologists and divers located the submerged wreckage of the Royal Tar resting in sixty feet of water off Vinalhaven. Embedded in the silt amidst copper hull sheathing and charred timbers, divers recovered brass passenger luggage tags, cutlery, English coins, and the heavy iron bars of the menagerie animal cages. Several artifacts were conserved and placed on permanent display at the Maine Maritime Museum in Bath and the Penobscot Marine Museum in Searsport.
The Wreck of the Royal Tar stands as an extraordinary chapter in American maritime history: a surreal intersection of frontier entertainment, technological failure, and raw human drama. It reminds us of a time when the world was wide and wondrous, when the arrival of an elephant on a wooden steamship could captivate an entire coast, and how in a single hour of terror, nature claimed both man and beast beneath the cold northern waves. The tragic memory of the circus ship remains etched into the granite coast of Maine, a haunting reminder of the fragile boundary between spectacle, hubris, and the untamed ocean.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The burning of the Royal Tar remains one of the most poignant and surreal chapters in American maritime history, honoring the lives of passengers and exotic beasts lost in the icy northern sea. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we travel to the Florida Keys for Henry Flagler's impossible Over-Sea Railroad.
